newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ORDERS SPAIN TO ACT QUICKLY IN GSM FEE ROW.
newsitem.headline: EU ORDERS SPAIN TO ACT QUICKLY IN GSM FEE ROW.

text.p: The European Commission told Spain on Wednesday it had until mid-March to announce how it plans to end distortion of competition in favour of partly state-owned Telefonica in the fast-growing Spanish mobile phone market.
The dispute concerns an 85-billion-peseta ($653 million) fee which the Airtel Movil consortium had to pay for the country's second GSM (Global System for Mobile communications) licence in 1995.
Telefonica did not have to pay for its licence in 1991, and the Commission said this gave it a competitive edge and strengthened its dominant position.
The European Union executive said in a statement the initial fee charged to Airtel -- which was selected after a tender -- harmed competition.
"In the absence of the licence fee imposed on Airtel, price competition would have been stronger and GSM tariffs would have fallen more quickly," it said.
The Commission has earlier intervened successfully in similar cases in Austria, Ireland, Belgium and Italy.
"We are giving the Spanish government three months to put the house in order," EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert told a press conference.
"It is up to the Spanish government to take a decision and it has to try to bring the situation back in line within three months, that is their legal obligation," he said.
Van Miert outlined three options for Spain -- the money could be paid back, which he conceded was "unrealistic", or the same fee could be imposed on Telefonica.
"That is a possible solution, it is fair enough, it has been done in other member states," Van Miert said.
But if this were not feasible, the third alternative would be to put together "a package of compensatory measures".
"To try to make up that package properly, the Commission is not just ready, but very keen to take part in any talks," he said.

Airtel is a consortium of banks, including Banco Central Hispano and Banco Santander, and other industrial and telecommunications partners, notably Airtouch Communications Corp and British Telecommunications Plc.
The Commission asked Spain as far back as April to refund the licence fee or compensate Airtel in other ways.

Madrid proposed transferring some costs from Telefonica to a subsidiary operating mobile phone services for the public operator, but it had not given the Commission sufficient data to allow it to consider the project equivalent to the fee.
The Commission had therefore decided to ask for "clarifications on the corrective measures the Spanish authorities intend to take in order to remove the distortion of competition."

In the earlier cases, Belgium, Ireland and Austria decided to impose a payment on the public operator while the Italian government proposed a package of corrective measures which was agreed by the Commission.
